subtopic: MB. BRACKEN-REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON MARCH 13
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On page 1355 of Hansard of yesterday the following words are credited to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon):
I do know that certain estimable and amiable gentlemen from the city of Winnipeg came to Ottawa-some of them I think are still here and are likely in this building tonight-with the objective of ruining this legislation, of killing this legislation one way or another. There is no doubt in the world that their first objective was to try to injure it and kill it if possible in the agriculture committee of this house. That opportunity was lost when the members on this side of the house, the members of the C.C.F. party and the members of the Social Credit party announced that they were opposed to this legislation, under all the circumstances, going to the committee on agriculture and colonization.
The minister continued:
Now it is my opinion-and possibly I might be blamed for imputing motives - that this attempt-
The amendment I moved.
-that this attempt to send this legislation back to the committee of the whole is merely another attempt, coming from the same quarter,-
The "estimable and amiable gentlemen" to whom he referred.
-to embarrass the government with this legislation.

At that point, Mr. Speaker, I rose and spoke as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman is suggesting improper motives.
A moment or two later the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I very carefully stated that I was not imputing any motives to anybody.
I suggest, sir, that the words just quoted from yesterday's Hansard do impute motives, and do impute them to me. In any event the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) raised a point of order, and Your Honour made a ruling. When I refer to that ruling I do so with all respect, Mr. Speaker. I have confidence that the rulings you make are your best judgment in the light of matters as you see them. This is what you said:
I listened very carefully to the minister when he was speaking and I listened to the hon. member who rose on a point of order. I do not believe that the minister imputed to the leader of the official opposition any improper motives. I understood that the motives were attributed to outsiders, not members of the house. Therefore, since he did not impute motives to any member of parliament, I do not think I could ask him to withdraw.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if you had had before you the words of the minister as they appear in Hansard today you would have given a different ruling.
In any event I need no defence in the province of Manitoba against insinuations such as those carried in the words used by the minister. .

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply with respect to the coal mining dispute in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Has the Minister of Labour any statement to make as to any progress being made in the settlement of that dispute? speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MARITIME COAL STRIKE-INQUIRY AS TO MEETING IN OTTAWA TO RECONCILE DIFFERENCES
speechtext:
I am not raising a question of privilege. If I did that sort of thing I would be on my feet twenty-four hours a day. Don't take yourselves too seriously. This morning I met a delegation of the Canadian congress of labour, -who made the suggestion that I call a conference of the parties concerned. I want to say, with all the emphasis at my command, that the Department of Labour is ready to conciliate this dispute at any time, if given an opportunity to do so. Might I say further that not only the people of the maritimes but I believe the people of the whole dominion wish to see this dispute brought to a successful conclusion.
As hon. members know, I appointed Mr. Justice Carroll as a commissioner, and he made certain recommendations. The position taken by the company was that unless they were guaranteed increased production they were not in a financial position to grant the increases requested by the men. The men took the view that an increase in pay should not be tied to guaranteed production. That is how the matter stands at the moment. Neither side has receded from its position. If at any time there is a spirit of conciliation, of willingness at least to give and take in the dispute, you may rest assured that I and my department will use every effort to bring it to an end. In my judgment, however-and of course this is a matter of judgment-there must be a spirit of compromise on both sides. To ask these people to come up here from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would be a waste of time, unless there were a joint request by both parties to the dispute.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH EMERGENCY LEGISLATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH EMERGENCY LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister indicated earlier in the week that I would be making a statement as to the probable course in iespect of the so-called emergency legislation. I have been waiting to see what the probable progress of the house would be
during the month of March, and I have come to the conclusion that in all probability it will be impossible for us to finish the emergency legislation on the order paper on or before March 28.
The National Emergency Transitional Powers Aet, 1945. as amended, will expire on March 29-not March 31, as is the general impression. It expires sixty days after the opening day of parliament. There is a substantial body of legislation which must be enacted before March 29, unless many important measures are permitted to lapse, thus causing a condition of great confusion, amounting almost to chaos, in the country. Therefore the government has come to the conclusion that it must ask parliament for an extension for a limited period of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, as amended. There is a proviso in the appropriate section of that act which states:
Provided that, if at any time while this aet is in force, addresses are presented to the Governor General by the Senate and House of Commons respectively, praying that this act should be continued in force for a further period, not in any case exceeding one year, from the time at which it would otherwise expire and the governor in council so orders, this act shall continue in force for that further period.
It was decided yesterday that there should be an Easter recess of nearly two weeks. That means that legislation which is uncompleted before the Easter recess will not be reconsidered before the fourteenth or fifteenth day of April. I think it would be unsafe for the government to plan for the completion of that legislation within a period of less than approximately thirty days after we reassemble. subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner for the second reading of Bill No. 25, to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening the minister spoke briefly after introducing this bill because, as he explained, he had taken the opportunity when the resolution preceding the bill was before the house to speak at some greater length as to the purposes of the measure. However, he did take the opportunity to explain that it was his intention when we reached the committee, stage to move an amendment which, as we understood, would have considerable effect on the measure itself. After asking him a couple of questions, which he answered, I sought and obtained the permission of the house to adjourn the debate a few minutes before eleven o'clock, in order that we might have an opportunity of considering what that amendment amounted to. The minister handed around slips describing it, but I must not discuss the amendment on the second reading. I should like to observe, however, that the effect of it will be to permit the distribution of apples, and apples only, whenever the distribution is undertaken by a board set up under a provincial marketing act. Further discussion of the matter will take place when the bill is in committee and we reach the section indicated.

Agricultural Products Act
The purpose of this bill is to empower the minister to lay his hand on certain agricultural products required for the purposes of international or other agreements which may be made. The methods by which that object may be attained are set forth in the bill, for the bill will empower the minister to establish a board or boards which will have very wide powers. Those boards will act under the direction of the minister and will be able to acquire agricultural products designated by the governor in council, deliver them, store them, and besides that, set the price which the farmer will receive for those products. That method of arriving at the object of the bill carries with it a principle with which we are not in accord. My mind goes back to the discussions which took place in this house in 1934 on the natural products marketing bill, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) fulminated violently against that bill from its first section to its last, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) expressed his strong opposition to its terms despite the fact that the farmers in the Annapolis valley had unanimously indicated their support of the measure. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what the situation would have been if that bill had contained these wide powers! Is it surprising that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) yearns for the day when the Liberal party may return to those principles which he alleges they once followed?
I say that we are not in accord with the principle involved in this bill. We do not consider it right that the farmer who produces the product should have no say in its disposition or in the price he shall receive for it, and in that regard we are on all fours with the representations made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture a fortnight ago today. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture met the government in the early hours of the day on which the minister moved the resolution which resulted in the introduction of this bill. The view of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is that the proper basis on which to proceed in such a matter as this is a recognition of those boards at present in existence or to come into existence under the marketing acts which have been passed in every province.
I want to point out to hon. members that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture speaks with no sectional voice in Canada. It neither speaks with the voice of one part of Canada nor speaks with the voice of farmers producing any one particular product. It is the collective voice of the farmers. There are branches of the Canadian Federation of
Agriculture in eight of the nine provinces. These branches meet annually and discuss their problems. They arrive at policies. Their delegates assemble here in the city of Ottawa and in open meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture they put forward their views, and the views of the federation are there hammered out, so that it is feasible for the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to meet the dominion government and set forth the policies which it advocates.
The main reason why I am so strongly in favour of recognition of the boards at present in existence under the provincial marketing acts is that they are producer boards. The basis of those nine acts is just this, that in any stipulated area, if there be a majority of producers of certain commodities who desire to form themselves into a board, they may receive permission to do so. They elect their board, and that board carries out the control and the regulating of the marketing of those crops in an orderly fashion for the benefit of the producer, the benefit of the consumer and the benefit of the trade, and it is only reasonable to my mind in a matter of this kind that the government should recognize the fact that such boards are in existence and that they are efficient. The minister himself has had opportunities of working with at least some of these boards.
I would draw attention by way of illustration to two things which have happened since the war began. When the war broke out, shipping disappeared so far as commercial produce was concerned. That was an extremely serious matter for the province of Nova Scotia because their habit for generations has been to barrel their apples and to send them across the seas to the United Kingdom, to Scandinavian countries, to Newfoundland, Iceland, and the West Indies. It was not such a serious matter for the apple producers in. British Columbia because for some years past from twenty-five to thirty per cent of their product had been sold in the export market, but it was sufficiently serious to deal a blow to that industry in British Columbia.
The only reason I am using the apple as an illustration is that I come, from the centre of the Okanagan valley and I personally am more conversant with the conditions of the British Columbia fruit trade than I am with those of the other boards which exist in that province. I would not like it to be thought, as has been alleged in times past, that the whole strength of the movement of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is based on the fruit industry, for that is very far from true. The fruit industry is merely one of those bodies which support the Canadian
Agricultural Products Act

Federation of Agriculture both in its provincial branches and in the federation itself.
When that export was entirely cut off, the federal government saw fit to make financial arrangements under which the farmers might be enabled to remain on their farms and to produce this food. That was a very considerable assistance in Nova Scotia. The method adopted was largely that of turning the apples over to the processors. In British Columbia it was necessary to a far lesser degree to make use of that financial assistance because as the war developed and as employment increased consequent on the spread of industry for the war effort, the domestic market reached such proportions that it was possible for the British Columbia fruit board to sell practically all its produce in the domestic market. But in that instance it is interesting to note that when the dominion government, having set up this financial arrangement, required some body of people to deal with it at the other end, it was to these fruit boards that they turned, and they made use of them in applying this financial arrangement.
May I give an illustration. Not long ago when shipping was again possible the United Kingdom indicated that it desired to purchase Canadian apples. The question arose as to where these apples could be obtained, in what quantity and what the price should be. The head of the British mission was directed to the two boards, the one in Nova Scotia and the one in British Columbia. He went to see the Nova Scotia board and the British Columbia board and carried out a dicker by the ordinary methods of trade with the one and the other as to quantity and the price that should be paid. Barrels of apples in Nova Scotia and boxes of apples in British Columbia when converted into barrels, turned out to be at very much the same price, and that price was the one which was adopted in the agreement with the United Kingdom. Therefore in these two matters the minister is not without knowledge and experience of what these boards are capable of doing. I would venture to suggest that he appreciates the assistance which those boards were able to afford in time of need.
We are not in accord with the principle behind this bill, because we believe that there should be recognition by the government of the existing boards, and it should be so stated in the bill. I intend to make that the subject of an amendment which I propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Charlton), and which I shall now read. It is as follows:
['Mr. Stirling.]
That the said bill be not now read the second time, but that it be resolved that an Agricultural Products Act should be based on the principle that producer boards, set up under provincial marketing acts, where such boards exist or as they may from time to time come into existence, be used for the purposes of such Agricultural Products Act, instead of commodity boards established by the minister under section four of the said bill.
The phraseology adopted in the amendment is the phraseology set forth in our rules of procedure for an amendment on second reading, but I should be extremely glad if the minister would see the force of the contention and incorporate that principle in the bill.
Under these nine provincial acts as they exist today there are a score or more of these boards dealing with all sorts of different agricultural products. Where there is a board dealing with a commodity which the minister desires to acquire it surely is but reasonable to give the producer of that commodity the opportunity to have a say in the disposition of the product as well as the price it will bring.
Now, an observation or two with regard to what the minister was good enough to divulge last evening in the matter of an amendment which he had in mind. I know that we must not discuss it at this stage, and I do not propose to do so; but I should like to make an observation or two with regard to it to show how it came about. When the minister spoke on the resolution which preceded the introduction of the bill it was getting pretty late in the evening and the house was good enough to assist him to the extent of passing rapidly through the resolution stage and reaching the introduction of the bill, because the following week the house would revert to the debate on the address and if we had not succeeded in getting the bill into our hands that night we should probably have had to wait a couple of weeks to see it.
As the minister drew to the end of his remarks I asked him the following questions as reported on page 930 of Hansard:
Did I understand the minister to say that the existing boards will be empowered only to carry out transactions connected with agreements which the government has entered into with other countries, or will this bill enable the boards to carry out other undertakings which they have taken on with regard to shipments out of one province into another province?
Mr. Gardiner:	The bill will cover interprovincial and international shipments.
Mr. Stirling:	Not only connected with the
agreement ?
Mr. Gardiner:	Not only connected with the
agreement. It does provide authority to deal with interprovincial transactions.
When we received the bill and were able to read it we could find nothing whatever in

Agricultural Products Act
it to warrant the minister in giving these answers; and in consequence the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, with three of his colleagues, called on the minister and asked him to be good enough to explain what the answers to me meant. On that occasion he told them that he had certain amendments in contemplation which he might move when the bill reached committee stage. He indicated that it would still be possible for the existing boards to carry on under the powers granted by the order in council under the War Measures Act, in the regulatory work which they had been doing outside the provinces in which these boards were set up. Again last night when the minister told us of the amendment that he proposed to move but did not indicate its character, he said that it would be possible for these existing boards to carry out regulatory work both in export and in interprovincial trade.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext: With regard to apples.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
Yes. The minister has restricted this amendment to apples, and although a small slice of bread is better than a whole loaf if you cannot get the whole loaf, it scarcely comports with what the minister is stated to have said to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when they met the government. I read these few words from the report got out by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on what took place during the discussion with the cabinet:
Mr. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, announced that he was introducing into the commons, an act which would carry on the powers and functions of various marketing boards which had been functioning during the war and up to the present. He indicated also that the act would convey powers which would make it possible for the government to meet part of the wishes of the delegation with respect to federal marketing legislation. However, he stated the act would only be in force for one year, to be reenacted again at that time if desired.
When we see the restrictions contained in the amendment, in that they refer to apples only and it is not by any means clear that they cover export trade as well as interprovincial trade, it leaves us with the doubt which we must carry in our minds until we reach the committee stage of the bill and can discuss them at greater length.
I therefore sum up in this way, Mr. Speaker. We quite realize that it is necessary for the government to obtain the commodities required for certain international agreements which they have arrived at, but we contend that before the disposition of the farmers' produce should be made, and particularly before the price is arbitrarily set by the minister, the farmers should have an opportunity of indi-83166-88
eating their wishes with regard to what they have produced and the price at which they are able to sell it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), but I regret that the acoustics of the house are such that I am seldom able to hear all that he says. I regret especially that I was unable to follow his entire argument in support of the amendment that he moved, but I hope that as I proceed I shall be able to gather the ends together where they may be somewhat apart. While he and I may deal with this question from different angles, I am certain we both have the sincere desire of doing something worthwhile for agriculture.
I should like to deal briefly with the general principles of the bill as they are outlined in the preamble. I shall read only that part of it which sets out what is really the main reason why the government considers it necessary to have this piece of legislation. I quote:
And whereas certain orders and regulations were made by the governor in council under the authority of the War Measures Act and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, for the purpose of enabling Canada to carry out the said agreements;

*
I might interject there, Mr. Speaker, that previously they were dealing with the agreements which the government had signed.
-And whereas the said orders and regulations will expire on March 31, 1947, and it is necessary by reason of the existing national emergency that parliament confer authority to enable the government of Canada to fulfil its obligations under the said agreements and to continue to sell and export food supplies to distressed countries for the relief of suffering and the distribution of essential food supplies, in order to maintain economic stability and to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace.
I should just like to emphasize that last part:
-"in order to maintain economic stability and to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace." I ask the government what period of time they would set as the transitional period. I think that is important. While the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) tabled some agreements today, I regret that we did not have them soon enough to get a little insight as to how long some of these agreements are to carry on. As I understand it, they are all for different periods of time, with the result that this act will be applicable for the purposes of one agreement which may be for two years and another which may be for a longer period. I should like to know what the government consider to be a reasonable length of time for the transitional period.

Agricultural Products Act

This bill is not what the organized farmers wanted or asked for. We had handed to us last evening a slip of paper which has quite a bit of typing on it, and which the Minister of Agriculture submitted for our consideration as an amendment to the bill which is before us. I shall not read the entire amendment; all those who are interested have no doubt read it. I consider it an improvement over what the minister had in the bill before, but if already he finds it necessary to submit an amendment to the bill, surely the bill in its original form did not receive all the consideration it should have received.
There is just the one point that I wish to emphasize. In paragraph (b) of subsection 5(1) of the proposed amendment of the Minister of Agriculture there are these words:
For the purpose of regulating the movement of apples from one province to another and requiring that any such movement be made only by or under the authority of a provincial marketing board.
That is all very good; but surely the organized apple growers of British Columbia and Nova Scotia and other parts of the dominion are in a much better position to make their wants known to the government than almost any other branch of agriculture which may be dealt with under this act. Yet apparently this was overlooked until just the last moment.
This bill does not go as far as the organized farmers want it to go. I would remind the house that some time ago we were discussing another related matter to which I hope I may refer without transgressing the rules of the house. While this matter was under discussion we were informed that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was holding a conference in the city of Ottawa, and we were told we should wait with the proposals being advanced at that time until we found out what the organized farmers wanted. Well, Mr. Speaker, other hon. members as well as I attended that conference, for at least part of the time, and I was pleased and more than surprised to hear the almost unanimous demand for legislation along the lines advocated by members of this group for quite a number of years. In their discussions they emphasized in no uncertain terms the fact that no longer should conditions be tolerated under which a small minority, for selfish reasons or otherwise, could upset orderly marketing for the great majority of the producers of certain commodities. In that connection I should like to quote briefly from an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of March 11, in reference to this conference. Here are the final sentences of the editorial:

The request for compulsory marketing agencies is not restricted to grains. The federation has presented the government with a draft of a dominion farm products marketing act. This bill calls for establishment of marketing boards to handle interprovincial and export trade in all agricultural products. And it has asked that the government bring it before parliament this session.
The federation's action indicates that the farmers have not the horror of planned marketing which some attribute to them. iRather they appear to believe that uncontrolled marketing holds greater dangers. No doubt they remember the confusion and starvation prices of prewar days. And they do not desire to have their livelihood again dependent upon the whims of market speculators.
Just to give an idea of what they think should be in a bill of this kind I am going to draw to the attention of hon. members, through you, Mr. Speaker, three portions of the draft bill presented by the federation. I need not bother with the sections or details, but will refer first to the short title. There they want the name to be "The Farm Products Marketing Act". May I mention in passing that the bill now before us makes no mention of being a marketing act. Furthermore, the federation specify this draft as-
An act to improve the methods and practices of the marketing of farm products in interprovincial trade within Canada, and in export trade, and to make provision for the regulation and control of trade and commerce therein, and to make further provision in connection therewith.
Then under "Purpose and intent" they say:
The purpose and intent of this act is to provide in respect to interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade, for the improvement of the methods and practices of marketing of farm products, in any or all respects and in whole or lation or prohibition of the marketing of farm products, in any or all respects and in whole or in part.
I submit that originally the legislation now under consideration did not contain provision for anything in respect to interprovincial trade, until the minister brought in his proposed amendment last evening. I should like to say a few words about the stand taken by the C.C.F. group in respect to orderly marketing during all these years. Time after time spokesmen for this group have placed before parliament our belief that, as I mentioned a few moments before, we should not have a condition under which a few, for selfish or other reasons, could upset orderly marketing for the great majority of the producers. That belief dates right back to the time we first formed our political association. In that connection I refer to a document, known as the Regina manifesto, drawn up at the first national convention held at Regina in July, 1933, setting out the policies and principles of this organization. I need not take

Agricultural Products Act
time to quote from that document except
that portion pertaining to the matter under consideration today, but I can assure hon. members that it contains some interesting proposals. Item No. 4 of the plank concerning agriculture deals with this very question. It says:
The substitution for the present system of foreign trade, of a system of import and export boards to improve the efficiency of overseas marketing, to control prices, and to integrate the foreign trade policy with the requirements of the national economic plan.
During all the years since 1933 we have been advocating this very thing; and as is pointed out in the editorial in the Ottawa Citizen which I quoted a short time ago, the organized farmers in more places than just the prairie provinces have come to lose their fear of orderly marketing. In that connection I might repeat something I have stated on more than one occasion, something which has been stated by many hon. members of this group. I refer to the urgent need for stability in the marketing of our farm products. I contend that this bill does not give the farmers the required stability. In the first place, I can foresee the possibility that this bill may expire a year from now, while some provisions, dealing with certain agricultural products, may run for a number of years longer. In the different branches of agriculture we need a much longer range view than that. We need long-range planning to give the stability I mentioned a moment ago. Take the dairy branch of agriculture, and see the position the dairy people will be in if they must plan only from hand to mouth, so to speak, or from one year to another. We all know that those engaged in dairying must be able to plan their work for some years in advance. Hog production does not need quite as long a time as dairying. Yet this bill does not give those who are connected with hog production any assurance that they will have a long-range policy, or that it will afford them any stability. Beef cattle require a longer period. It takes from two and a half to three years for producers of beef cattle to cash in on their work.
In the matter of fruit, we have a type of farming in which a number of years are required before the farmer begins to realize any advantage from the work he has put in; therefore he needs a longer time in which to plan. Even vegetable growers require stability and planning in their markets. I am happy to say that they too are beginning to realize the necessity for controls and regulations. The great need is for coordination and control of interprovincial as well as export trade, and above all the desirability of as 83166-88J
great a degree as possible of democratic control by the producers themselves. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the re-drafting of this bill to make provision for:
(a)	A dominion marketing board to have control over the orderly marketing of any farm product in interprovincial trade within Canada and in export trade;
(b)	Authority to confer on any existing local marketing board or agency established under law of a province, power to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovincial trade and export trade;
(c)	The establishment where any provincial local marketing board or agency does not exist, of local marketing boards to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovineial trade and export trade, providing the establishment of such a board, is favoured by a majority of the producers in the area concerned, the membership of such a board to consist of producers of the regulated product in the area to which this scheme relates."

The point of order which I intended to raise was not in regard to the amendment to the amendment; it was in regard to the amendment. Citation 755 of Beauchesne's, second edition, reads:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the
bill.
The amendment reads as follows:
That the said bill be not now read the second time, but that it be resolved that an Agricultural Products Act should be based on the principle that producer boards, set up under provincial marketing acts, where such boards exist or as they may from time to time come into existence, be used for the purposes of such Agricultural Products Act, instead of commodity boards established by the minister under section four of the said bill.
Reference is made to section 4 of the bill. If an amendment in these terms is to be moved to the bill the proper place to move it would be when that section is before the committee, not on the second reading. I suggest that section 4 provides for exactly what is suggested in the amendment. Action may be taken not only under the bill but under another act, and I refer to chapter 29 of the statutes of 1944-45, which is the Agricultural Prices Support Act. There is, under that act, the possibility of setting up boards which would do identically the same thing as is provided for in the bill we are discussing.
In other words, there are two different ways of dealing with the transition. We may deal with the transition under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, as we are doing in the case of potatoes, or we may deal with other products in other ways. That act provides in paragraph (i) of section 9:
The minister under regulation passed by order in council has power

Agricultural Products Act
(i) to appoint commodity boards or other agents to undertake the purchase and the disposition of agricultural products.
Under that section we can appoint any agency that has been set up by any organization to undertake the purchase and sale of farm products. In the section referred to in the amendment it is provided that we may utilize the section of the other act for the purpose of setting up boards. If I am permitted to do so under the rules of the house, I should like to read the last part of section 4 which states:
The minister may direct that any agricultural product designated by him may be purchased for the purpose of this act or the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, only from a provincial marketing board.
In other words, where those boards do exist for the handling of products it is possible for us to do exactly what the hon. member for Yale thinks we ought to do. The bill provides for that. There are products dealt with in agreements for which no provincial boards exist. Apples happen to be the only product where there is a complete organization set up right across Canada by the producers to deal -with the situation. I submit that the amendment does not change the legislation; it simply advocates something already provided for in the legislation. Second, it is an attempt to amend a section of the bill which can be amended in committee if we so desire. Such an amendment should not be considered on second reading as an amendment to the motion for second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of this bill I should like to quote a few words written by a member of the wheat pool and found in the Agricultural Institute Review of September, 1945, at page 28:
With the floor price legislation proposed we now have two opposing policies offered to Canadian agriculture for the post war years. The first policy is the laissez-faire, do nothing, take it on the chin, rugged individualistic stupidity we have experienced in the past, and under which, when the depression becomes too severe, we unfortunately have a war to pull us out of the economic mess.
I think, after the vote that was taken last night, we can take it for granted that there are only seven members of this house who believe in that type of policy. In considering this bill which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has placed before the house today, I think hon. members are anxious to try to get the best bill they can for agriculture in this transitional period and for the years to come.
Therefore I think anything said in this discussion can be taken as an honest effort on the part of hon. members to create better conditions for the industry of agriculture in this country.
As to the principle of the bill, I do not think much exception can be taken to it; at least we in this group take no exception to it. However, we believe that principle cannot be carried into effect by the bill in its present form, since it is merely to cover a transitional period. As yet no one has been able to define what that transitional period is. I can remember quite well coming back after the first war and taking up land under the soldier settlement board. I remember the drop in prices of agricultural products which took place in 1921, and then the gradual rise from 1924 to 1928. We thought we were through with the transitional period by that time; we thought we had got over the effects of that war. In the latter part of 1928 and in 1929, however, we found we had only begun to feel the effects of the war. Today how can we judge what will be the transitional period? Is this bill constitutional? If a case is taken to the courts in a year or two from now, will the courts decide that we are still in a transitional period? I do not know, and I do not LMr. McLure.]
believe the minister knows. Therefore I believe this bill should do more than just carry on certain orders in council during the transitional period. It should give some stability to agriculture in this country. I know of cooperatives in the old country who wish to establish purchasing agencies in this country, who would like to start to build up business contacts here, but who are doubtful, under this transitional form of legislation that has been introduced in Canada with respect to the marketing of agricultural products, whether it would be advisable for them to make the necessary investments here, not knowing just how long we might carry on under our present forms of marketing. Therefore, instead of bringing in this order in council legislation, which is about what it amounts to, I think the government should have brought in something more definite and more permanent, which would give the necessary assurance of stability to our agricultural industry at the present time.
As to our floor price legislation, we do not know where the floor prices are to be set. They may be fixed at a level which will give a reasonable return to agriculture, and again they may not. When the floor price legislation was introduced the Minister of Agriculture had this to say, as reported at page 5612 of Hansard jor 1944:
Then I should say it would be unfair to the farmer immediately to require him to sell at the cost of production, without considering at all any losses he sustained because of the war or any returns he was denied through the controls established during the war. The suggestion was made that farmers had been denied returns in the earlier part of the war and that just at the time when in the ordinary course of events, according to the experiences of the last war, he would have reaped some returns which would have been helpful to him, ceilings were placed upon prices, as a result of which he *was denied as great a return as otherwise he might have received. All those matters would have to be taken into consideration during the transition period along the lines I have suggested.
In this legislation there is no indication that this will be done; that is why I feel the bill should be more definite. That is why the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) moved his amendment, which did add certain new principles to the bill. That amendment was ruled out of order because it deleted the Conservative amendment. Now that the Conservative amendment has been ruled out of order, I believe our amendment will be in order. I therefore move, seconded by 'the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of

Agricultural Products Act
this house the government should give consideration to the redrafting of this bill to make provision for:
(a)	A dominion marketing board to have control over the orderly marketing of any farm product in interprovincial trade within Canada and in export trade;
(b)	Authority to confer on any existing local marketing board or agency established under law of a province, power to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovincial trade and export trade;
(c)	The establishment where any provincial local marketing board or agency does not exist, of local marketing boards to administer any scheme of the dominion marketing board in respect of interprovincial trade and export trade, providing the establishment of such a board, is favoured by a majority of the producers in the area concerned, the membership of such a board to consist of producers of the regulated product in the area to which this scheme relates.
This amendment has two purposes, the first of which is to see that the bill covers interprovincial trade. The bill, as it was presented by the minister, contained no reference to interprovincial trade, except in the amendment he tabled last evening. That amendment refers to one specific product, but that is not sufficient to meet the needs of agriculture in Canada at the present time. That was the statement made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at their recent meeting in Ottawa. I have in my hand, their brief, in which they say this interprovincial provision is necessary in connection with beans, peas, milk and a great many other agricultural products where small groups of growers, perhaps not more than five or ten per cent of the total number, were marketing their products outside the province and thereby spoiling the work of the commodity board controlling the product within the province. So I believe that provision should be extended, by concurrent legislation or, if the dominion has the power, by the dominion transferring that power to the provincial board in some way, to prevent this interference with the work of provincial boards in the marketing of their products. I am not a lawyer; I do not know where the constitutional authority lies, but I know that either the province or the dominion must have it, because the dominion has any residue of powers not given to the provinces. Therefore the federal government should be able to eliminate this difficulty which the provincial boards are meeting at this time. If it can be done with regard to apples, which from the amendment introduced by the minister I judge it is proposed to do, I see no reason why it cannot be done in connection with other products as well, and I believe the act should say so clearly.
The other point in which this amendment differs from the bill is that we state definitely that the boards set up under this legislation will be producer boards, that the growers of the product within the area in which the board is set up shall compose the board. That can be varied; if a majority of the producers wish to elect someone else to the board, well and good, but certainly the producers themselves should have control over the local marketing boards. That is a democratic principle which we cannot get away from, and something which should be included in the legislation. This legislation can never wTork successfully until it has the full cooperation of the producers of the product to be controlled. It goes without saying that a thousand ways would be found of getting away from the regulations and orders of the board, if the producers themselves are not behind it.
We think the only way the producer can or will be 100 per cent, or to any appreciable percentage, behind the scheme, is by seeing that the local boards are under their control. That has been the policy of this group for many years. We say that the producers themselves should have the domestic control of their product. When it comes to a matter of exporting, where the producers themselves go into the export market; and where products are being produced in different provinces, that is the place where the dominion government should step in, coordinate the work and see that the exporting is done on the basis of the Canadian economy, and not on the basis of provincial economy.
Those are the reasons why we move the amendments. W7e think they are good amendments, and we say they should have the support of the house. I say the Minister of Agriculture on behalf of the government should be prepared to accept such a reasonable proposal, which is in the interests of agriculture in Canada.

control the Agricultural Products Marketing Act. They say that they want the same thing as we do, practically, namely, that the farmers should be permitted to control the sale of their own products. I do not know when this change came about, but apparently it has been quite recent. Whether or not it is a case of their trying to follow the demands of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, I do not know and I should not like to say. Nobody can accuse me of changing my mind in the house in that regard. I have been definite at any time that I have said anything on it. I am not in favour of government control. If there has to be any control, then the farmers should be allowed to control their own destiny.
So far as this bill is concerned, there is no doubt in my mind, although I may not be able to read into it what the minister can read in it, that it is purely and simply government control of farm products. Evidently the minister himself can read into the bill what was asked for in the amendment which we moved; but it is not there for me to see. There are too many "mays" in the thing for me to take it at its face value. Surely the minister does not think the farmers of Canada are so helpless that they cannot run their own business. At least I hope he does not think so. When given half a chance they have done not a bad job in the past, except during the depression, which was not their fault.
Contrary to the statement of the minister as recorded on page 937 of Hansard, this bill does not give the Canadian Federation of Agriculture what they have asked for; hence by our amendment today we endeavoured to point out to the government that the producer boards as set up under the provincial marketing acts should be allowed to conduct their own business, instead of having it done for them by government controlled commodities boards, as set forth in the bill.
I should like to quote a portion of Mr. Hannam's address which has been referred to often in the house. The meeting was held in Ottawa at the Chateau Laurier on February 26 of this year. This is just part of what he said, in speaking of the type of marketing for which they were asking;
This type of marketing is midway between state marketing such as the Canadian wheat board, and purely voluntary associations of farmers for marketing purposes. Instead of state marketing with state regulations, state financing and state management, we are asking the state to give groups of producers a chance to do their own marketing. It is essentially a self-help procedure.

Agricultural Products Act
The minister may say that the farmers of Ontario may not want this. To prove that the farmers of Ontario do want it, they have set up the following schemes under the provincial marketing act: cheese; asparagus growers;
pear,	plum and cheery growers; peach growers; vegetable growers; including tomatoes, green
peas,	sweet corn and green or waxed beans. They have a seed com growers association; a sugar beet growers marketing scheme; a berry growers marketing scheme, and the last, a hog producers marketing scheme. During the next month or so I believe there are three or more to be voted on, which include cream producers, grape and soya bean producers. I contend that the producer himself as represented by the producers boards should have some consideration when prices are being fixed by contract for the products which he produces, under this bill. As it stands, the minister seeks the authority to make contracts either with government or government agencies or agencies of any kind to fix the prices and actually to confiscate, seize or, in any way he so desires, to get hold of that product to fulfil such contracts at a price fixed by the minister himself.
As I said before, the minister may be able to read into this bill certain things that are not clear to us. I hope he can; I hope he does that, but it is not satisfactory to us. He says, it is there and he can use it if he wants to. We want to make it definite that it will be used and not left to the discretion of the minister as to whether he will use it or not.
During the war years the farmers accepted controls as part of their war effort; but now that controls are being lifted on many of the articles the farmers buy, they are being asked to accept the maintenance of controls by the government on the produce they have to sell. As I said before, if we must have controls, let the farmers themselves do the controlling. I think they are the people who should do the controlling, if there is to be any control. I can assure you, sir, that it would be much more conducive to good will and understanding among governments, producers and consumers if this were done. If this bill is an indication of what the government's agricultural policy might be, it is only fair to warn the government that there will be a greater number of farm sales in the country and a good many more acres of good soil lying idle in the next few years.
The producers of Canada are now being asked to produce and deliver to Great Britain many products at prices which are less than the English farmer himself is obtaining for those products. I am not saying that we should not supply those products to England at the prices at which we are supplying them,
for the sake of the British people. But if Canada wants to do that-and it is a wonderful gesture on the part of Canada-let the Canadian people as a whole bear the burden and not the farmers alone. I believe the farmers have always accepted their share of responsibilities without receiving a fair share of the returns from their product. I believe this bill discounts the ability of the organized farmers to bargain for themselves. It obviously does that. It is easy enough for government officials to sit back and say what is best for us; but I believe the producers themselves, if given the opportunity, are quite capable of doing a worth-while job for themselves, for the consumers of this country and for the world at large. I would therefore strongly urge that the government give every consideration to the wishes of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and allow them the privilege of doing their own marketing.

Speaking to the amendment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to point out some of the inconsistencies that are apparent in connection with the discussion which has been going on since this afternoon. Earlier in the session, when the provisions of other bills were before this house dealing with the orders in council which were utilized throughout the war for the purpose of doing things which neither this government nor any other government would desire to do in peace time, the position was strongly taken, particularly by the official opposition, that nothing new should be introduced into any of these bills. That is, we had orders in council which were passed for certain purposes under the War Measures Act, without in some instances having received first the assent of parliament to their being brought into effect. It was stated-and persistently- that in any legislation which was introduced, in order to make for a limited period of time those orders in council applicable to the transition period between war and peace, it was to be taken for granted that this house-and particularly members of the official opposition, in so far as they could prevent it, would not permit any new legislation being tacked on to any of the bills which were brought to the house in order to carry out the intent of making these orders in council applicable to the transition period.
Now we come to the House of Commons on this occasion, when the government has hesitated to put anything into this bill whatsoever which would be new legislation; we hesitated to the extent of not even providing for the marketing of apples under the agreements, through the fruit boards which have been set up by the provinces and organized nationally right across this country.
But in the discussions which took place in connection with the resolution, members in different parts of the house, and more particularly those of the official opposition, raised questions with regard to the fact that full provision was not made for that purpose in the bill. This warranted us in believing that the house would agree that to that extent we could depart from the general principle which was insisted upon in connection with all this legislation, and that we might bring into the legislation something which had not previously been provided for in the marketing of apples.
We have gone that far. I would say that the bill has introduced, in the slightest degree possible, some new ideas into the application of orders in council, for a limited period after the war is over.

I do not think it would be proper to do that-even if the government desired to do so, any more than members of the official opposition thought at the beginning of this session it would be proper to do so. If and when legislation is brought down to deal with marketing on the basis suggested by the farm organizations, it should not be legislation which has in it provisions to deal with orders in council which were brought in during war time, which were applied during war time, and which are still being applied.
Why were these orders in council brought in, in the first instance? They were brought in so as to make it possible for the government, by compulsion, to take farm products and to send them to Great Britain for the purpose of assisting in the prosecution of the war, for the feeding of our own soldiers, for the feed-

mg of the British people; indeed, for the feeding of any of the allied forces wherever they might be fighting.
To indicate what we did do under that legislation, let me point out that we went into Ontario and into Quebec and took all the cheese produced between May and October, in two different years of the war; we took all of it, and shipped it to Great Britain. We did not leave any of it here, at all. And at other times we used the authority we had under the act to go into packing plants and take the bacon, and to say to our own people, "You can have in this country only fifty per cent of what you were buying in 1940. The remainder of it is going to Great Britain."
In other words, the orders in council covered by this legislation have in them powers which I doubt very much even members of the socialist party would desire to have in legislation which is to be passed for the purpose of dealing with a situation which will arise in peace time.
We are suggesting in this legislation that for one year we be given authority to continue to do what we were doing in war time. We are not saying that everything we did during war time will be done; but we are saying, or suggesting, that the authority we had during war time should be allowed to us for one more year.
Then I suggested, on the resolution, that in all probability because of the fact that our contract extends through 1947 and 1948-two of them at least through 1949-we shall be coming back to parliament at the end of each one of those years asking for a continuation of the powers as they are related to any of the contracts still in existence. I said, we presumed that, at the end of each of those years, if circumstances warranted it, parliament would give us that authority.
There are persons belonging to the same group who, in this house, ever since the session began, have been saying that these compulsory powers ought to be taken away from the government, and that we should not have them. Then we have the suggestion made tonight that this bill, which is intended to continue only for one year, with authority to come back here and remodel it in order to take care of anything still to be taken care of, should at this time provide for a permanent marketing organization. If it is to satisfy the farm organizations it could not be anything other than a permanent bill.

You will find that most of these bills are put into effect by order in
council. There is very little legislation put on the statute books at any time that any government has any authority over that is not put into effect by order in council. In every bill that goes through this house provision is made for the government to make regulations and to do certain things by order in council. And the same would be true of any bill that may be passed with relation to the marketing of farm products.
The point I wish to make at the present time is this. There are persons who have been talking against compulsion being put into any of these measures or authority given to the government to compel, and who at the same time are talking in favour of a bill which goes much farther in the direction of compulsion-I am not saying whether I am in favour of it or otherwise-than most of the measures that have been before this house. What does this proposed bill provide for? It provides that if the majority of the farmers producing any farm product decide that they want to market their product a certain way, then everyone else in that community must market his product in that way.
These orders in council have given the government authority to go into the market at Montreal and take cheese and send it to Great Britain. They give the government authority to go to the packing plants and take the bacon and send it to Britain and agree to pay what it is worth. We have had that authority throughout the war; we have had that authority in connection with practically all farm products, and that is provided under the orders in council. We are suggesting putting that into a bill.
But the proposed legislation says that wherever the majority of a group of farmers, locally if the organization is a local one, provincially if it is a provincial one, and nationally if it is a national one, vote in favour of marketing a product in a certain way, then everyone else may be compelled to market his product in that way. I do not know how you could carry compulsion much farther than that, or compulsion that strikes at the individual to a greater extent. Again I say that I am not arguing-it has nothing to do with this bill-whether that is a good thing or a bad thing, but I wish to point out that if this last amendment, which I have not had time to read, is in order and carries, and if the legislation is sent to a committee to be changed in the manner suggested in the amendment, then this legislation passes out altogether and we get a new bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
It might be. But you should not do away with this bill while you are doing that. The better bill my hon. friend speaks of will not deal with the present situation and could not. I will explain why. There is only one board in this country which is organized on the basis that is suggested by the farmers across Canada, and that is the fruit board. The fruit board is organized provineially in Nova Scotia; it is organized provineially in British Columba; it is organized provineially in Ontario and elsewhere. It has a central organization which meets from time to time to discuss the problems of the industry and to submit its views on the apple industry to those concerned. There is no such organization as that in relation to bacon; there is no such organization as that in relation to cheese; there is no such organization as that in relation to eggs; and there is no such organization as that with regard to any farm product affected by the orders in council other than apples.
Therefore, if we were put in the position tomorrow of not haring this bill so that we could go out and get farm products to supply the British contracts, of course we would not
Agricultural Products Act

be able to continue to supply those contracts. If we came to the middle of May, as has been suggested, or, as it stands now, if we come to the 29th of this month without the enactment of this legislation, we would have no authority to go out and obtain the products that are necessary to supply the British contracts in any of those commodities referred to in the orders in council. So I say, Mr. Speaker, the house seems to have got away from discussing what is involved in the second reading of this legislation and to have been discussing something that is not involved here at all. Hon. members have been disoussing whether we should have a marketing bill for all time in the Dominion of Canada. I submit that that is not the question which is before the house and that all the discussion in regard to it is entirely out of order. There is no motion before the house with regard to a marketing bill for farm products. There is no possibility of changing this bill into a marketing bill without destroying the results which must be obtained if we are to supply the British contracts. There is no possibility of doing the one thing without destroying the other. Consequently, if we are to have both things done, they must be done in two separate bills, and an attempt should not be made to put the other project into this bill. The farm organization realized that when they brought their representations before the government. This afternoon I quoted from the representations which they had made. It was this:
(1)	A dominion farm products marketing act is essential to the economic welfare of agriculture, the basic industry of Canada.
(2)	In effect the authority and control which would be provided by such legislation were established and employed by the dominion government during the war years and subsequently as emergency measures in order to secure maximum production and efficient distribution for the purpose of fulfilling overseas commitments and contracts which had to be honoured.
They said that we had most if not all of the authorities under the orders in council passed during the war with regard to a certain number of products, but they applied only to a certain number; and' they said that they wanted legislation which would apply the same authorities or the greater part of them to all farm commodities in Canada. Then they said they had a method to suggest by which that might be done.
(3)	Such legislation will be a major factor in providing stability for agriculture through the medium of orderly marketing, domestic and export.
(4)	Such legislation will conduce to proper planning by agriculturists over the time or period of years which their particular branch of primary production demands.

Therefore be it resolved:
That this conference convened by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture with representatives of major agricultural organizations in attendance from all sections of the dominion ask that the directors of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convey to the dominion cabinet the unanimous request of this meeting that legislation in line with the attached draft of a farm products marketing act, be introduced at the present session of parliament.
That is the submission made to the government. Attached to it is a model bill which provides for the authorities that I mentioned a few moments ago. It provides that this government set up a dominion marketing board; that we pay the costs of operating that board; that through the operation of the board we direct the activities of export and interprovincial trade in farm products along certain lines.
What was the answer given to that request? In 1930, the first month or so, of the war, the farm federation came to us with the same request. If I remember correctly, in 1939 there were only three or four provinces

I have forgotten the exact number-which had provincial marketing legislation. Since that time, all the provinces have adopted provincial marketing legislation. Nine provinces have set up legislation under which provincial marketing boards can be established. As every hon. member knows, the activities of the provincial marketing boards are confined to marketing within their own province. What is suggested is that we should set up a board which would take over the control of interprovineial and international marketing of farm products. When that suggestion was made in 1939 I made a statement to the farm federation at that time. The man who is president now was the president then. I said, "I am not prepared at this time, and the government is not prepared, to discuss with you the pros and cons of marketing legislation. We have just entered upon a war and that war makes it necessary for the government of Canada itself to set up boards to take control of the marketing of the farm products of' Canada in order to ensure that our own people as well as our allies have the proper proportions of the food which is produced in this country and in order to induce greater production so that we may be able to feed greater numbers during this war period."
Of course the logic of that was agreed to by the farm organizations. From 1939 down to this year the organizations have not asked for that legislation. They have kept continuously reminding us of the faot that provincial legislation has been passed first by one province and then by another, and that

Agricultural Products Act
eventually they would be coming to Ottawa to ask for legislation. Personally I think this was the right year for them to come. This is the first year that we have been entirely away from the war in so far as shooting is concerned, but we have not yet got through the transitional period. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) wants to know when we are to get through it. Well, I will give him the same reply that I gave when the same question was asked-I am not too sure that it was not by the same hon. member-in 1944 when we brought in the legislation which is intended to take care of the transitional period. On that occasion I said that the transitional period of the first war did not really end until 1930, 1932 or 1933; that nobody could be absolutely certain when the transitional period will end. I went on to say that many people contended that it did end in five years; others contended that it did not end for twenty years, but someone will have to make a decision some time as to when the transitional period ends. We cannot do it now.
Some people have suggested that we put four years in the bill; some have suggested that we put five. We finally decided not to put a term of years in it at all. But I want to say quite candidly that if we can so regulate the marketing of farm products in this country as to give a proper deal to the farmers and to the consumers without applying the terms of the floor prices bill to too many products, then we hope to be able to do that. One of the ways in which we hope to be able to do it. is to retain, so long as it is essential to do so, the agreements with Britain which we have covering the marketing of farm products which we can see will be surplus for the years that are ahead of us that will assure to us the British market for the surplus production of farms in this country. Therefore we are asking at this time for authority to continue these agreements under this special legislation for at least one more year. At the end of that year we can come back and state what the conditions are and we shall probably ask for the continuance of it for another year. But if the times ever comes-and we hope it will not-when agreements such as we are now utilizing for the purpose of assisting farmers over the transitional period are not available to us at levels which make it possible for us to carry out our obligations to the farmers, then it will probably be necessary for us to make the floor prices legislation more widely applicable, and make those effective throughout the remainder of whatever the transitional period is.
I am not going to attempt to answer the question of the hon. member for Humboldt tonight as to how long the transitional period will last. I only know that it is still with us and, if I read correctly the discussions which took place not later than either this morning or yesterday, and which are reported in the papers tonight, on the floor of the House of Commons in Great Britain, then I am inclined to think the transitional period is still with us with a vengeance; because there are some people in the House of Commons in Great Britain who think the farmers of this country are making great profits at the expense of people who live in Great Britain. We have not realized that. We do not believe it. As a matter of fact, we think the farmers of this country are making a real contribution to the feeding of the British people, to the feeding of the European people and to the feeding of others who are short of food in different parts of the world. We feel that we are doing this at a less cost to the people concerned than they are being supplied from any other part of the world. That being so, I think it is time for someone to say that when a man stands up anywhere in the world and says that Canada is trying to make profits at the expense of someone else, either he is talking about something he does not know anything about or he is speaking with some intent other than that of serving the people of his own country.
This legislation is to deal, not necessarily with the whole transitional period but for a part of it; and the only part that we can say with definiteness at the moment that we hope it will continue in existence to deal with, is to take us through the bacon contracts which run to the end of 1949, to take us through the beef contracts which also run to the end of 1949; to take us through the contract on dairy products, which up to date runs us down to the end of the 1947-18 period, and which we expect will carry us on through a period similar to the other two contracts. We hope that a similar arrangement will be made with regard to apples; that by a cooperative arrangement between Great Britain and this country we shall be able to get reasonable returns, not necessarily as high returns as the farmer in Britain receives unit for unit of the different products produced in that country because their costs of production are not necessarily the same as ours-there are reasons why they are not-but will give us returns which bear a reasonable relationship to the prices which are being paid by the British to their
Agricultural Products Act

own people and a reasonable relationship to the prices which are being received by people in some of the other parts of the world.
May I say again that we have been carrying out that idea, that we have been supplying food to Britain at a lower cost-as every member in- this house has been saying, some of them agreeing with it and some of them disagreeing-than other people in the world have been supplying it up to the present time. And I say quite candidly that we expect that over the entire period of the three or four years during which these contracts last we shall have a reasonable return, as compared with other peoples in the world from that market which we believe to be our best market, our most secure market, and the one in which we have the best chance over a long period of time of being paid for our commodities.

Although I did not mention it at the time, in view of the question which has been asked, I will mention it now: for five years we are told that we can have a market in Britain for all the beef we desire to send them.
Those facts being the case, all we are asking the house to do at this time is to pass this legislation to give us authority to go on with the provisions made in the orders in council, over a sufficient period of time to permit of our carrying out the contracts which we have with Britain. We are asking for nothing more than that. We believed that in bringing the bill down in its present form we were asking for what this house wanted us to ask for, particularly the opposition, namely, only the authority to do under this special legislation what we had been doing under the War Measures Act. We are asking no authority to do anything else. Therefore I object to any attempt being made by the house now to put into this act terms which never were intended to be in legislation of this kind; terms which, if they are to be enacted at all, ought to be enacted under separate legislation brought into the house, discussed on its merits and if this is the proper time to pass it, if it must be passed, then it should be passed. But if it is not the proper time to consider it, in view of the fact that organizations are not yet prepared to do the job that is required to be

done, then it could be brought in at some other time by whatever government is then in power.
But we submitted this argument to the farm organizations, and so far as I know the farm organizations accepted the argument and did not expect legislation this year. However, I would submit that they do expect legislation as soon as they can get it and would take it this year if they did get it. I am quite certain that they do not expect it this year but rather that they expect that with these powers under this bill, and with the extra power which has been asked for in connection with apples, we could go through this season without bringing any great hardship upon any one, even to the extent of not doing injury to the views which they hold with regard to compulsory marketing of farm products. So I would suggest that we discuss the bill on its merits and not discuss all kinds of amendments which would put this bill completely out of existence and call upon us to bring in some other form of legislation to deal with the permanent situation.
