speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened for some considerable time to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) criticize other members in the house for straying from the bill; but probably because of the portfolio he holds, he has himself led us into pretty far and green fields. I shall try to answer some of the arguments which he put forward with such violence and vehemence. He first criticized the official opposition because he said there was incon-

Agricultural Products Act
sistency in our attitude. He criticized us because, as he said, we now asked him to import into this particular bill matters which are foreign to the purpose of the bill, which is merely to place in statutory form those things which previously have been done by order in council. He went on to say that it would be improper to do anything more at this time or to import any other matter into the bill.
I take some issue with the minister in that respect. It is true that we in the official opposition have pressed for the cessation of legislation by order in council. I make the distinction again between administration and legislation. We have pressed for the end of the practice of doing by order in council what should properly be done by act of parliament, and of giving to ministers, or boards set up under ministerial authority, power to make rules having the force of law perhaps contrary to some existing statute. We had hoped to see introduced legislation to replace the orders in council passed under the War Measures Act. That is the type of legislation which we had hope to see in Bill No. 25. But what we find, Mr. Speaker, is not an act putting into statutory form what has hitherto been done by order in council, but an act giving authority to continue to do by order in council what we say should be done by statute.
That is the first distinction I would make, that this bill gives to the minister just as wide powers as he ever had under the War Measures Act or under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act; and there is no point therefore in his objection to our criticizing the bill and saying that we wish to see this thing put on a regular and permanent basis. We desire to see a proper marketing act and enabling legislation brought in, not legislation simply under the guise of a regularizing act to continue placing in the hands of the minister power to do those things which should be done by parliament or some duly constituted authority subject to the control of parliament.
In support of my contention I would refer to section 3 of the bill. Without reading it in detail, I may say it gives the minister power to sell, to buy and to store; it gives him sole control over the price level, and control over the quantities to be marketed, in connection with all agricultural products in the Dominion of Canada with the exception of wheat. The producers are given no voice in setting the price, in the quantity to be bought or in the marketing of their product. That is why I say, instead of regularizing powers or giving powers back to parliament, this bill simply continues
a situation to which we have objected in the past; that is, it gives the minister and the governor in council power to do things which should be done by and subject to the control of the House of Commons. That is the answer I would make to the minister's first objection. There is no inconsistency in saying we should have a marketing act that is a marketing act and not an act which simply makes the minister the buyer, the seller and the sole authority over markets in Canada.
Second, the minister said he was not taking any very great powers under this bill, and that therefore the charge that he was seeking to set himself up in sole control of agriculture was not well founded. I asked him, what about the power to continue the contracts or make new contracts? He said, "What we are going to do under section 3 is to continue the contracts already made. We are giving ourselves wide powers under that section, but we will not be exercising them. We do not really need them, and we do not intend to exercise them." When taxed with this again, however, he went on to say, "Well, we are not ' exercising very wide powers, except occasionally the power to negotiate new prices." Some hon. members, he pointed out, were pressing for new prices under some of the contracts; and he said some of the contracts would be going on until 1949.

I hasten to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that my reflection, if there was any, was not directed at Hansard. I thought I was stating a fact, that occasionally the things we hear and the things which appear in Hansard do not resemble one another, and I was leaving it at that; I believe that is a mere statement of fact. I did hear the minister say in effect that there would be no substantial creation of new contracts. He went on to say, however, that there were contracts
Agricultural Products Act

which took us up to 1949, and I suggest that, as situations change, these contracts will require to be revised, and under the terms of this bill the person to revise them will be the minister, without reference to the producers or to parliament. He comes in here with an agreement already signed, brings this legislation before us and says, "We have to have it in order to carry out these contracts. If you oppose it you will be besmirching'the good name of Canada, because without it we cannot live up to our obligations to another country."
With regard to the question of giving powers which it is said are not intended to be exercised, this whole question was up in the house as long ago as 1934, when the Bennett government introduced its marketing act. It is significant to note the extremely violent, vitriolic attacks which were made, not only upon the legislation but upon the ministers introducing and supporting it. They were represented as villians and rascals of the first order, who were seeking only to abuse their power and to grind the country under their heel. One of the hon. gentlemen in the opposition at that time who made an attack on the legislation upon these grounds is the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). I should like to read what he had to say at that time in regard to giving these wide powers to ministers and ministerial boards. I quote from page 2210 of Hansard for March 16, 1934:
We cannot assume that the drastic powers which are conferred upon the government by this measure will not be exercised. Some of those in my constituency who urged that I support this bill have said:	"Yes, these powers are
exceedingly drastic, and we can understand how in their working out great injustice might be done or great inconvenience suffered, but we must not assume that the government will misuse the powers granted under the bill or need not assume that the government will invoke those powers."
Then he went on:
I do not think a member of parliament should vote to confer powers the exercise of which he disapproves. For this reason I am afraid that I shall have to oppose the bill as it stands.
The minister is in his place in the house at the moment, and I would be very glad to hear from him as to whether he still feels the same way about conferring powers the exercise of which we do not approve, even though we have the assurance from the minister that it is not intended to exercise these very wide powers. I for one agree entirely with the remarks of the right hon. Minister of Justice at that time, and I hope he still feels the same way.

The Minister of Agriculture ended up with the point at which he started, and said that in introducing a measure of this sort to regularize the emergency powers exercised under the War Measures Act and the transitional powers act it would not be proper to seek to introduce a full-fledged marketing act. He gave as one reason that this is a transitional measure, that these conditions may be entirely transitory, and that what he is seeking to do is take care of these transitory conditions. However, in almost the same breath with which he was saying this was only a temporary measure he went on to say that he could not give any assurance that he would bring in a marketing act because, he said, after the last war these transitional conditions continued for ten years or more, and they might go on this time for four or five years. The minister seems to envisage a pretty permanent transitional measure, and if it is to endure for as long as he forecast tonight, then instead of constantly continuing emergency powers I think he should do now what the farmers of this countiy are pressing for, and bring in a proper marketing act which would give the producers of this country control over their produce and their processes, instead of leaving it exclusively in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture.
One other point in the minister's speech was significant, and I should like to comment on it now, and shall refer to it again later in my remarks. We saw him make once more an effort to hold over the head of the official opposition the big stick of the contracts with Great Britain. The minister said, "If you oppose this bill you will be denying to us the powers necessary to carry out our contracts." For my own part, Mr. Speaker, I object strongly to what I thiffir is cheap legislation; legislation which, under the guise of giving powers necessary to carry out contracts signed by the government of Canada, introduces provisions for all sorts of extra and additional powers which in our view should not be given; powers which certainly are not necessary for the carrying out of these contracts; and in connection with which we are then told, "If you oppose the bill, if you oppose it in its entirety or in part you are taking away from us the power to carry out these contracts", and therefore holding us up in the light of being anxious to besmirch the good name of Canada, and to jeopardize the discharge of responsibilities undertaken by the government of Canada.
It is cheap on two grounds. It is a cheap way of getting excessive powers which the government wants, and it is a cheap effort to

Agricultural Products Act
place those who conscientiously oppose many of the things done by this bill in the light of being opposed to the preservation of the good name of Canada.
Well now, having said that, in so far as the minister's speech is concerned-because I felt many of the things which he said should be answered-I should like to speak with regard to the bill itself now before the house. It is difficult to discuss this bill on second reading, because its very principle is so difficult to find. I think that was illustrated this afternoon in the rulings which were given with respect to the two amendments which at various times were before the house.
An effort was made to find the principle of the bill, and to introduce amendments which would be contrary to the principle, or to suggest opposed principles. Each time Your Honour found in the amendments no sufficiently clear distinction between the amendments and the principle of the bill to bring the amendments within the rule, and on that ground they were ruled out of order.
It seems to me that that is a proper criticism to make of the bill, and it arises from the fact that under the guise of seeking to carry out a contract with Great Britain a great deal more is introduced than is necessary to bring about that purpose. After careful examination, however, we cannot say that the principle of the bill is only to carry out the agricultural agreement made with the United Kingdom. If it were that, no one would oppose it. There is a great deal more than that.

speechtext: There is nothing more than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
The principle is not to be found in the title. The title gives the purpose; it is to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products. I am following here a distinction made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself in 1934, when he was discussing the Natural Products Marketing Act introduced by the Bennett government of that day. At that time the Prime Minister carefully distinguished between the purpose of the bill and the principle of the bill, and no one questioned his distinction. The Prime Minister of that day agreed with it, and all hon. members in the house agreed with and accepted it.
The principle is not to be found in the preamble; again that seems to define the purpose. Then, it is not to be found in the title, or in section 1, nor is it found in section 2, the definitions section.
I suggest it is not until we come to section 3 that we get any inkling as to the principle behind the bill. And when we study section
3 carefully we find the principle of the bill is to enable the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to control the marketing and sale of all Canadian agricultural products, with the exception of wheat. That is the first principle of the bill-to give that control to the minister. A secondary principle is found in section 4, which enables the minister to establish one or more commodity boards. This being so, I suggest that we have to examine section 3 closely to understand the full import of the principle of the bill.
Paragraph (a) of section 3 gives the minister power to sell all agricultural products in Canada. Paragraph (b) of that section gives him power to buy on behalf of foreign countries any agricultural products in Canada. Paragraph (d) gives him power to store any or all agricultural products in Canada.
So we find the minister in the extraordinary and preferred position of being both buyer and seller. He is the czar of all agriculture in Canada-not the producers, themselves; they have no say in the prices or quantities of their produce sold-the Minister of Agriculture is to have the whole say in this sphere. That is my main objection to the bill, namely, that the producers of Canada will have no control over their produce, or their activities in selling them or marketing them. The Minister of Agriculture alone controls those features.
The second provision which I find objectionable is the one which gives the minister power to conclude new treaties and new agreements with other countries without reference to parliament. One of the features to which wre have already taken objection is the fact that this parliament is thus placed in the position of having to accept the whole of these measures, because included in them is one particular power, namely the power to carry out agreements already made. That was the position we were in with respect to the wheat board act, and the position we are now in with respect to this bill, because there is meat; there is beef; there are bacon, and eggs which are already the subjects of agreements with Great Britain. And I object to that principle wherever it is found.
I object to parliament's becoming nothing more than a rubber-stamp to carry out the predetermined policies of the Minister of Agriculture. He goes to these countries and makes agreements with them as to prices and quantities. Then he comes back to parliament and says, "I have made this agreement; this is the price level, and there can be no question about the agreement. You must accept this legislation in order to enable me to carry it out."
Agricultural Products Act

I can just hear what would have happened if this party had been in office and had introduced similar legislation, and the same hon. gentlemen who sat on these benches in 1934 had been facing the government which was trying to get this legislation through. I can just hear the minister who comes from Vancouver Centre; the hon. member for Quebec South; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) and the Prime Minister, who excelled themselves then; and I somehow feel they would have done even better tonight in their attack on this bill, had it included these powers.
I want to read what the Minister of Justice, who was perhaps the most reasonable, being a lawyer, of those who made the attack in 1934, had to say. Let me read what he said with regard to taking away the powers of parliament in this matter. Speaking on April 16, 1934, he is reported at page 2212 of Hansard in this way:
One by one measures are introduced which take away the powers and authority of parliament. I certainly cannot approve, nor do I think my constituents or the producers of this country will approve, of the taking away from parliament of its time-honoured rights and privileges, its function of legislating for and protecting the interests of all classes in the community.
Well, what is the provision under the bill now before us? Have producers any say in the marketing of their commodities? They have only such say as the Minister of Agriculture, in his goodness, may give them. He buys; he sells; he stores; he sets prices- and he sets the prices before the consumer and before the producer knows what is going on. Then he comes back to parliament and says, "I have made an agreement; I have set the price, and you will have to ratify it." And parliament not only is in a position where it cannot hold the minister responsible, but cannot take any step it wishes to take on behalf of the producer, if he thinks his price is too low; because we have seen in the last week that, if we make any effort to remedy the situation, deliberately we are held up as being those who are trying to make it impossible for the government to carry out its sacred word. So I say that is another of the principles of the bill, another feature in it, which is most objectionable. I think it should be provided that in future no agreement made by the Minister of Agriculture with any other country shall be valid until it is ratified by parliament. I think the proper way to proceed would be to have the producer boards control this thing, not the minister. We have introduced an amendment which would serve that purpose but it has been ruled out of order.

Nevertheless, our view is that the producer boards should have this power and then there would probably be no objection.

Agricultural Products Act

On May 28 of last year I spoke at some length on the question of national farm marketing. I do not intend this evening to repeat my arguments or illustrations, except to say that I think the decision of the conference of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which was held in Ottawa recently proves the validity of the arguments I put forward at that time and the illustrations I gave, as to the stand of the farmers of this country behind this legislation.
With other hon. members I had the opportunity to attend one morning session of that conference, and I must say that it was even surprising to me to see the unanimity which was expressed regarding this question of national farm marketing legislation. It was not sectional, although this idea, I am proud to say, originated in British Columbia. The idea was supported from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast. I do not think I have ever attended a farmers' convention in which there was expressed such general agreement on a principle. I am not going to quote the resolution carried by that conference. The minister has already read it to the house and it is on our records, which I think is a good thing because we shall want to refer to it in the future. But I wish to refer briefly to three or four points. I think the action of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture conference, which shows that there is unanimous support across Canada for this type of legislation, proves that the people who are directly concerned with this legislation support it and desire it, and desire it and demand it now.
Second, it is definitely democratic. While we use the words "compulsory marketing legislation", I personally do not like that term; I think it is democratic marketing legislation because it is the decision of the majority of the industry concerned.
This conference in Ottawa was not produced as a result of short-term action on the part of the people. What happened in Ottawa recently was the result of this matter being discussed for years by the small local organizations of farmers throughout the country. The decision of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture conference in Ottawa was a decision which was arrived at as a result of the work, the will and the activity of the rank and file; it was a decision produced from the bottom up and not from the top down.
Then, again, I think this type of legislation has proven its worth from experience, and I am not going to take the time to go into that. We in British Columbia know, after some years of experience with this type of legislation, it has been the salvation of the
[Mr. Hcrridge.J
fruit industry and has put that industry at the present time on a sound financial footing, provided that we get the type of legislation which is required in the future to supplement provincial marketing legislation. I think that is admitted generally.
Another point, Mr. Speaker; at this time many of us are concerned about the youth of this country returning to the farms. I am one who is very much interested in the building up of the rural population of Canada, because I believe that so long as we have healthy rural communities and a prosperous agriculture, we shall continue to have a democratic and prosperous Canada.
Many of us are particularly concerned in seeing that the young veterans returning from the last war particularly have an opportunity to become established on the farms. We find that many boys raised on the farms- I have some of them in my own district and in my own constituency-are hesitant to locate on farms. Why? Because they want to be assured of some measure of security in the future. I say-and I think I shall receive general agreement in that respect-that if we can have the type of legislation demanded by the farm organizations of Canada we shall at least be showing these boys that we are doing all that is within our power and under our control at this time to secure for them a satisfactory living on the farms in the future.
I must say that I cannot understand the attitude of this government, a Liberal government which professes to support free enterprise. I say that this government, professing the principles of free enterprise, has, in recent months, struck some heavy and lusty blows at democratic enterprise in this country, and by its failure to bring in this national marketing products act legislation is causing a great deal of delay in democratic action by farmers in Canada. I am speaking tonight not only as a member representing the constituency of New Westminster, but also as a member of the Pacific Poultry Association. I know full well, in the days past when we had a surplus of eggs, the tragic situation which arose with regard to price. No wholesaler would take the risk of taking a small shipment of eggs, going across to Great Britain and finding a market four or five thousand miles away from British Columbia, with the result that, on occasion, eggs dropped to a price as low as eight cents a dozen. Poultrymen went out of business and in many cases lost all they had.

Mr. Speaker, I am a modest sort of fellow and do not like to express opinions unless I know a little about the subject with which I am dealing. But since there are, evidently, so many immodest people in the chamber, I thought I might as well take a flyer too.
As I have followed the debate which has taken place in this chamber in connection with this bill, my understanding is that the principal difference between the members of this group and the government is that this is a temporary measure, special bill for one year, and we believe that is not what is called for at the present time but rather a measure that is more or less of a permanent nature. Whether that point of view is correct I do not know, but I do know that,

when this bill expires, whoever may be minister of agriculture will be compelled- because circumstances will not be any different at the end of the year from what they are now-to introduce a bill that will do what we have been trying to do this afternoon. My point is that I am not sure whether or not this is the time to introduce such a measure. If that cannot be done, of course I shall support this bill, and I think my colleagues will do likewise. But we believe there should be more comprehensive legislation now7.
As a matter of fact, the farmer is not seeking government assistance in marketing because he likes to have government assistance. He is seeking it because he has no other choice. The individual farmer today is not dealing with individual buyers but with large and powerful organizations. He is helpless in selling his products under those circumstances. He has, therefore, no choice but, first, to organize as farmer and producer groups, and, then, to seek through legislation, both federal and provincial, to obtain orderly marketing of his products. The farmer is compelled today to do what the industrial worker has done over the last 100 years; that is, to organize to sell his products. The industrial worker, having no property except his labour, could easily see where and how he was exploited. The farmer, having a certain amount of what he called property, required a fairly long time to understand that he was being exploited in the same way. He has now arrived at the point where he realizes that, and he is creating organizations for the orderly marketing of his products.
I was interested in some parts of the speech of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I happened to be here in 1934 when the Bennett government was trying to get its marketing legislation through parliament. My hon. friend is quite correct when he says the Liberal party opposed it most strenuously. They debated the matter day after day, night after night, week after week, enlarging upon the dangers of government control and all that sort of thing. So much were they opposed to it that when the legislation was finally passed they took it to the courts, which declared it ultra vires. The only difference I can see now is that my hon. friends are doing the very same thing the Liberals did when they were in opposition in 1934. Referring to the fine of S5,000 provided in this act, as compared with the fine of S500 in the other legislation, my hon. friend asked, "Are the members on the government side of the house ten times as socialistic as they were in 1935?'' Well, if the enlarging of the fine is

Agricultural Products Act
the measure of their socialism, perhaps they are; but a great deal of water has gone under the bridge since 1935, and while my hon. friends on the opposite side of the house may not be as bright as those on this side, they have learned some things in those ten years. But there is another factor entering into the picture; that is, they are faced with the responsibility of administering the affairs of the country, and you cannot be as irresponsible on the government side of the house as you can be on the opposition side. That is something we do not always keep in mind.

Well, I do not know. I have a feeling I have tried to be responsible since I came inito this house. I may not have succeeded, but at least I have .tried. I did not get much of an education; there were too many potatoes to dig, too many berries to pick and, when there was nothing else, there were stones to pick, so that there was not much time to go to school. But I had a fairly good training in the shorter catechism, and I have a good idea of what is it to be honest, so that I can never bring myself to the point where I can be irresponsible just because 'the other fellow has the responsibility; and I am in the same position now. I have said that I think what this group is asking for is reasonable; it will have to be done some time, and .the only question is whether this is the time to do it, and whether this is the time we should try to force it to be done. If it is not, then we shall support this bill.
But let me get back to the point I mentioned a moment ago, as to the measure of the socialism of my hon. friends opposite. If the Conservatives in 1935 favoured legislation of this kind and the Liberals opposed it, and the Liberals favour it now while the Conservatives oppose it, does that mean the Conservatives in the house today are ten times less socialistic than they were in 1935?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARD

I do not think I am able to define exactly what is socialism, but really it means the social organization of the efforts of the people of the community to provide for themselves. What may be called socialism today and denounced because it is socialism, tomorrow will be considered good and accepted because it is good, because it serves the needs of the community; as a matter of fact, because we cannot get along without it. Personally I 83166-90
have never been able to see that there was any great merit in leaving the resources of the country in the hands of a few people, because there was something democratic and fine about it, and. making the _ mass of the people go to those few to obtain access to the economic life of the country from their hands. I was brought up on a farm. I have tried farming; I know what it is like. This is what I found. When I went to sell farm products, butter, eggs, lambs, potatoes, oats, pork and and so on, I always asked the man to whom I was selling the products, "What are you giving for this today? What is the price of potatoes today? What is the price of pork?"
But the funny part of it was, when I went to buy from these same people, I also asked what was the price, the price of the things I wanted to buy. So that the farmer, under conditions of that kind, got it, as the saying is, both coming and going. No wonder he has been skinned beautifully down through the years.
Just one point further; in regard to a statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I do not think I can agree with him-and I do not think he will, when he thinks it over-when he says that we must put all the details of marketing into a bill. I do not think that is possible. We would have so many clauses, sections and subsections that it would not make sense when you finished with it.

I cannot contradict the hon. member, because I did not see the legislation. But my personal opinion, for whatever it is worth, is that you cannot put all the details into a bill. Circumstances change from day to day, and the person or persons responsible for the administration of the legislation must have a certain amount of leeway so that they may be able to manoeuvre under those circumstances. If they are to be bound by legislation in an act, they just will not be able to do what it was intended they should do. So that I believe that, while the act should be as explicit as possible, we must, in the natural order of things, leave a certain amount of leeway to whatever board or minister, or whatever other officials are administering the act.
Let me repeat that this group will support this legislation. But we believe that what is required now is not merely an emergency bill



Agricultural Products Act
for one year, but a measure which will meet the needs of the producers of this country for some years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to try to add further to the confusion. I rise at this time for the purpose of trying to get a few things clear in my own mind. First, I should like to say that when I first came to the House of Commons I was under the impression that I was entering the national parliament of Canada, a body which legislated for the whole country, on an equal basis. But I find, since coming here, that, instead of sitting in a national parliament, which should aim at the equalization of conditions in the country as a whole, I am sitting in a form of nine little parliaments of Canada, each of which is endeavouring to do everything it can for its own particular province. After my experience here, that is pretty much my conception of parliament at the present time.
A few minutes ago the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) rose in his place and spoke for his constituency. That is what he is here for. But, in addition to that, he talked about the west, and the extreme west. That is all very fine, too. Then he made reference to the great prosperity of the east at the expense of the west. For his benefit let me say that, so far as the extreme eastern section of Canada is concerned, that portion from Quebec to the east, his statement would not apply; he was thinking in terms of central Canada, the exploiting machine of the whole country.
The extreme eastern section of the country is in pretty much the same position today as in Europe-after having come through a war. It is on relief. It is 100 per cent unemployed, because of neglect in the field of labour relations on the part of the national government. Today they are going from coast to coast, seeking relief for the persons in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. They have chaos, and no one is trying to do much about it.

Check up on your Minto mines, after a seven weeks' strike. I say this for the purpose of bringing to the attention of hon. members wrho emphasize conditions in the west, that I am thinking in terms of Canada as a nation. This is a national forum, and is supposed to look after the difficulties of the east and the west on an equal basis.
With respect to the present legislation, naturally I shall support the bill, because it is a step in the right direction. A minute ago the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said it was a hesitant step on the part of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Well, I hope that, before this parliament prorogues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will take equal steps, no matter whether they are considered hesitant or not. I would hope that they would take those steps in the industrial field. I consider the step now being taken in respect of the marketing of agricultural products on a national basis is a long step forward.
This is not the farmers' problem; it is an economic problem. It affects the whole of Canada, and ramifies into all its economic processes. A minute ago the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) stated that the measure was necessary to protect the farmer, because he is an individual, and that the worker had done a similar job for himself a good many years ago. I do not see it in exactly that way. Under his cooperatives, and the like, the farmer has been organized for a long time. But when he had to go out barehanded and deal with Canada Packers, Swifts or the grain exchange, he was in exactly the same position as the industrial worker is in, whether organized or unorganized, when he has to deal with the same Canada Packers, Swift Canadian, British Empire Steel and Coal, General Electric, and such others of the few large organizations which control all the economic processes in this country.
As I said a minute ago, I hope similar legislation will be brought in by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to protect the fields covered by his department, including, for example, the marketing of lumber and the establishment of a national fuel policy for the regulation and sale, and the import and export of Canadian fuels, so that we shall be in the same position as are the farmers, with their boards.
I hope the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will introduce a bill to set up a coal board, for the purpose I have mentioned; also to supervise the millions of dollars spent

from the national treasury in the fuel industry, and to see that that money is spent in a manner whereby there will be supervision of imports and exports. That is not being done in industry today. That is why there has been industrial unrest. I hope, too, that the Minister of Labour will take a leaf from the book of the Minister of Agriculture and bring in a bill to establish national labour.
